query: For an FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy protective coating susceptible to progressive plastic deformation during continuous loading, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its creep resistance? Specify the governing factor and rationale, an unspecified controlled comparison that would reveal it, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, the operating boundaries under sustained stress, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: The creep resistance of the FCC/BCC high-entropy alloy protective coating is primarily governed by the formation of nano‐scale precipitates or a serrated grain boundary morphology at the phase interfaces that impedes dislocation climb and motion during continuous loading.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-deposited FCC/BCC dual-phase high-entropy alloy protective coating with largely straight, unpinned grain boundaries.
generation.intervention: A controlled post-deposition heat treatment designed to promote either nano‐scale precipitate (e.g., L12) formation within the FCC phase or grain boundary serration at the FCC/BCC interfaces.
generation.conditions: Sustained high-temperature (up to around 900 °C) continuous loading conditions that induce creep deformation.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanostructural features at the grain boundaries and phase interfaces (serrated grain boundaries and/or finely distributed precipitates) acting as dislocation pinning sites.
generation.mechanism: The modified grain boundary morphology or precipitate formation increases barriers for dislocation climb and motion, leading to a more homogeneous strain distribution and delaying the onset of accelerated creep.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared with the baseline as-deposited coating, the treated coatings will exhibit a lower steady-state creep strain rate, a longer creep rupture life, and a more uniform distribution of strain in microstructural analyses.
generation.baseline: The untreated, as-deposited FCC/BCC coating with predominantly straight grain boundaries and minimal precipitate-induced pinning.
generation.boundary: The effect is expected to operate under conditions of high temperature (approaching 900 °C) and sustained mechanical stress, where progressive plastic deformation is of concern.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative impact of grain boundary serration versus nano‐precipitate volume fraction is not fully defined, and the interplay between the two mechanisms in improving creep resistance may vary depending on the processing parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FCC/BCC high-entropy alloy coatings: one set receiving a tailored heat treatment to induce grain boundary serration/nano‐precipitate formation and a control set maintained in the as-deposited state with straight grain boundaries. Subject both sets to identical high-temperature (≈900 °C) creep tests under continuous loading conditions. Use transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to characterize microstructural evolution and measure steady-state creep strain rates for each set.
measurements: Grain boundary morphology and precipitate size/distribution via TEM
Dislocation density and distribution via electron diffraction techniques
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the heat-treated coatings do not demonstrate a statistically significant reduction in creep strain rate, a delay in the onset of accelerated creep, or improved microstructural stabilization (i.e., no significant difference in grain boundary serration or precipitate formation) relative to the control coatings, the hypothesis that these microstructural modifications govern the creep resistance is falsified.

## Abstract
AbstractIn aero-engine applications, turbine blades operate under high-temperature and high-pressure thermomechanical cyclic loading conditions, which demand exceptional mechanical performance. High-entropy superalloys, characterized by a stable dual-phase γ/γ′ microstructure, have emerged as promising candidates for high-temperature structural materials due to their superior creep resistance. In this study, the creep behaviors of high-entropy superalloys are systematically investigated using molecular dynamics simulations, exploring the effects of stress, temperature, γ/γ′ lattice misfit, and γ′ volume fraction on creep deformation mechanisms. The results show that both stress and temperature significantly influence creep behavior, with temperature exerting a more dominant effect. As the applied stress increases, the dominant creep mechanism evolves from atomic diffusion to dislocation nucleation and motion, eventually leading to phase transformation. Additionally, the γ/γ′ lattice misfit and γ′ volume fraction are found to critically affect the alloy’s creep resistance. ## Abstract
ABSTRACTIn this study, tensile and creep deformation of a high-entropy alloy processed by selective laser melting (SLM) has been investigated; hot ductility drop was identified at first, and the loss of ductility at elevated temperature was associated with intergranular fracture. By modifying the grain boundary morphology from straight to serration, the hot ductility drop issue has been resolved successfully. The serrated grain boundary could be achieved by reducing the cooling rate of solution heat treatment, which allowed the coarsening of L12 structured γ′ precipitates to interfere with mobile grain boundaries, resulting in undulation of the grain boundary morphology. Tensile and creep tests at 650°C were conducted, and serrated grain boundary could render a significant increase in tensile fracture strain and creep rupture life by a factor of 3.5 and 400, respectively. Detailed microstructure analysis has indicated that serrated grain boundary could distribute strains more evenly than that of straight morphology.
